claims.text: The investigated material is a single-crystal FeNiCrCoCu coating on a single-crystal Cu matrix.
The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating is a stable FCC solid solution.
The initial coating has low dislocation density.
The initial coating has high stacking-fault energy.
Above 900 K, enhanced lattice diffusion produces stress-assisted dislocation climb in FeNiCrCoCu/Cu.
Dislocation climb above 900 K causes rapid dislocation annihilation and starvation.
Increasing thermal entropy lowers the free-energy barrier for kink-pair nucleation.
The alloy has low stacking-fault energy at high temperature.
Low stacking-fault energy at high temperature promotes an FCC-to-HCP transformation.
Collapse of stacking-fault networks mediates the FCC-to-HCP transition.
Disordered HCP clusters coalesce into an amorphous surface layer.
The amorphous surface layer lacks the work-hardening capacity of the FCC lattice and therefore sharply lowers hardness.
The amorphous surface layer promotes adhesive wear and material transfer, causing the friction coefficient to spike.
The friction coefficient decreases between 300 K and 600 K because dislocation annihilation increases the elastic modulus.
The friction coefficient spikes above 900 K in correlation with HCP formation and amorphization.
Wear resistance drops precipitously above 900 K as deformation changes from dislocation-mediated plasticity to diffusion-controlled amorphous sliding.
At lower temperatures, dislocation glide and twinning dominate and maintain high hardness and wear resistance.
The high-temperature friction and wear transition is caused by thermal disorder rather than mechanical annealing.
Polycrystalline FeNiCrCoCu systems may instead be dominated by grain-boundary sliding.

contradictions.description: The initial state is assigned high stacking-fault energy, whereas the mechanism invokes low stacking-fault energy at high temperature without stating or supporting a temperature-driven reversal.

The hypothesis attributes HCP formation both to collapse or annihilation of stacking-fault networks and to low stacking-fault energy. Because stacking faults commonly generate local HCP signatures, annihilating them would tend to reduce rather than create the proposed HCP population.

The endpoint is described simultaneously as an HCP-rich state, an HCP phase, and an amorphous state. A genuinely amorphous region lacks long-range HCP order, so these labels require a staged or spatially separated interpretation that is not clearly specified.
